---
title: "Environmental Systems and Ecological Change（环境系统与生态变化）"
---

## Forests as Functional Ecological Systems（森林作为功能性生态系统）

A forest functions as an integrated ecological system（功能性生态系统）that holds soil, regulates water, stores carbon, shelters species, moderates local climate, and supports the continuous movement of energy and nutrients. Its visible form includes trees, branches, leaves, roots, animals, insects, fungi, and soil organisms. Its deeper value comes from the relationships among these elements and the functions they perform together. A forest operates as a network of interdependent processes（相互依赖的过程）that maintain conditions suitable for life across multiple scales — from the microbial community（微生物群落）in a single gram of soil to the regional climate patterns shaped by transpiration（蒸腾作用）across thousands of square kilometres of canopy.

The canopy（树冠）slows rainfall before water reaches the ground. Leaves and branches reduce the force of falling raindrops, allowing water to enter the soil more gradually. The litter layer（枯枝落叶层）on the forest floor absorbs moisture and protects the surface from direct impact. Roots stabilise soil（固定土壤）, create channels for water movement, and help the ground retain structure. Fungi and microorganisms（真菌和微生物）break down dead leaves, wood, and organic remains, returning nutrients to the soil. Birds, insects, and mammals support pollination（授粉）, seed dispersal（种子传播）, predation（捕食）, and decomposition（分解）. Each of these processes depends on the others: decomposition releases nutrients that support plant growth, plant growth provides habitat and food for animals, animals disperse seeds and pollinate flowers, and the resulting vegetation maintains the canopy structure that regulates the microclimate（微气候）beneath it.

These processes form the ecological functions（生态功能）of a forest. A forest regulates the water cycle（水循环）, supports soil formation（土壤形成）, provides habitats（栖息地）, maintains biodiversity（生物多样性）, stores carbon（碳储存）, and moderates local climate（调节局部气候）. Each function depends on relationships among living and non-living parts of the system. Trees shape the soil environment; soil supports plant growth; plants support insects and animals; animals influence plant reproduction; microorganisms recycle nutrients; water movement connects the entire structure. When one function weakens — for example, when canopy loss reduces water regulation — other functions are affected in sequence: soil dries, seedlings die, habitat simplifies, and species decline.

Forest structure（森林结构）creates multiple layers that support different forms of life. The upper canopy receives sunlight and reduces heat at ground level. The understory（林下层）contains smaller trees and shrubs that provide cover for birds, mammals, and insects. The forest floor holds fallen leaves, seeds, fungi, insects, and decaying matter. Below the surface, roots and soil organisms form a hidden network that controls nutrient cycling（养分循环）and water storage（水分储存）. These layers create many microhabitats（微栖息地）, allowing different species to live within the same physical area. A single hectare of tropical forest may contain hundreds of tree species, thousands of insect species, and millions of individual organisms, each occupying a specific position in the vertical and horizontal structure of the forest.

Habitat（栖息地）functions as the set of conditions a species needs for survival and reproduction. For a bird, habitat may include nesting sites（筑巢地点）, food sources（食物来源）, protective cover（遮蔽结构）, seasonal temperatures（季节性温度）, and nearby water. For an insect, habitat may depend on a specific host plant（寄主植物）, soil moisture, or breeding surface. For a tree, habitat includes light availability, soil nutrients, rainfall, temperature range, and relationships with mycorrhizal fungi（菌根真菌）. A forest supports species because it provides many overlapping sets of survival conditions（生存条件）. The structural complexity（结构复杂性）of a forest — multiple canopy layers, diverse plant species, varied microclimates — creates more habitat niches（栖息地生态位）and therefore supports more species.

Biodiversity（生物多样性）expresses the richness of life inside an ecosystem through the number of species（物种数量）, the variety of genetic traits（遗传特征）, and the range of ecological roles（生态角色）. A biodiverse forest contains plants with different root depths, flowering times, seed forms, drought tolerance, and growth patterns. It also contains insects, birds, fungi, reptiles, mammals, and microorganisms that interact with those plants. This diversity gives the forest resilience（韧性 / 恢复能力）— the capacity to absorb disturbance and continue functioning.

Resilience（韧性）allows an ecosystem to absorb disturbance（吸收扰动）and continue functioning（继续运行）（生态系统承受扰动并继续运行的能力）. A forest with many plant species responds to drought（干旱）more flexibly, because some species tolerate dry conditions better than others. A forest with several pollinator species（传粉者物种）continues plant reproduction even if one insect population declines. A forest with diverse soil organisms（土壤生物）maintains nutrient cycling under changing moisture or temperature conditions. Diversity creates alternative pathways（替代路径）inside the system. When one pathway weakens, another pathway continues part of the function. This functional redundancy（功能冗余）is the mechanism through which biodiversity produces resilience.

A simplified ecosystem offers fewer alternative pathways. A monoculture plantation（单一种植林）may produce timber or crops efficiently in the short term, because one species can be planted, harvested, and managed at scale. Its internal structure is usually less diverse, so it carries higher ecological risk（生态风险）. A pest outbreak（虫害爆发）, drought, disease（疾病）, or fire（火灾）can spread quickly through a uniform system because every individual shares the same vulnerability. The same trait that makes production efficient — uniformity — also makes the system vulnerable（脆弱）to any disturbance that targets that uniform trait.

Deforestation（森林砍伐 / 森林清除）alters several forest functions simultaneously. Tree removal reduces canopy cover（树冠覆盖）, exposes soil to wind and rain, decreases root support, removes habitat structures, and reduces the amount of organic matter entering the soil. Once the canopy is removed, rain strikes the ground with greater force. Surface runoff（地表径流）increases, and water carries away fine soil particles. This process causes soil erosion（土壤侵蚀）. The erosion rate after deforestation can increase by a factor of ten to one hundred compared with rates under intact forest, depending on slope, rainfall intensity, and soil type.

Soil erosion reduces soil fertility（土壤肥力）because the upper soil layer（表层土壤）contains much of the organic matter and nutrients required for plant growth. When this layer is lost, the land becomes less able to support vegetation. Plant recovery slows, exposed ground expands, and future rainfall causes further erosion. Sediment（泥沙）may enter rivers and streams, changing water quality（水质）and affecting aquatic habitats（水生栖息地）. Through this pathway, tree removal influences soil, water, plants, animals, and human communities in a cascading chain of effects（连锁效应链）.

Deforestation also changes the local water cycle（局部水循环）. Forests help water enter the ground through root channels and organic soil structure, return moisture to the atmosphere through transpiration, and maintain humidity（湿度）within the local environment. When vegetation cover decreases, less water is absorbed by roots and released by leaves. The land may become drier, local temperatures may rise, and streams may receive more irregular flows after heavy rainfall. In the Amazon basin（亚马逊盆地）, researchers have found that deforestation reduces regional rainfall because less moisture is recycled through the forest canopy — a feedback mechanism（反馈机制）where forest loss causes further drying, which causes further forest stress.

Habitat loss（栖息地丧失）follows when forest structure is simplified, fragmented, or removed. Species that depend on tree cavities（树洞）, dense shrubs, leaf litter, shaded streams, or particular food sources lose the conditions that support their life cycles. Some species can move into nearby areas if suitable habitat exists. Others depend on specific conditions and decline when those conditions disappear. Specialist species（专性物种 / 高度依赖特定环境的物种）are especially sensitive because their survival depends on a narrow range of food, shelter, climate, or breeding conditions. A toucan that requires large fruit-bearing trees for food and tree cavities for nesting cannot survive in a cleared landscape even if some trees remain.

Habitat fragmentation（栖息地破碎化）appears when a continuous forest is divided into smaller patches by roads, farms, settlements, or cleared land. Fragmented habitats create edge effects（边缘效应）. The edge of a forest receives more sunlight, wind, and human disturbance than the interior. Temperature and humidity change near the edge, and many interior species（内部物种）lose suitable conditions. Fragmentation also makes movement harder for animals. A population divided into small isolated groups has fewer mating opportunities, lower genetic exchange（基因交流）, and greater vulnerability to local extinction（局部灭绝）. The minimum viable population（最小可存活种群）— the smallest population size that can persist over time — may not be met in small fragments, leading to progressive species loss.

Carbon storage（碳储存）represents another major forest function. Trees absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis（光合作用）and store carbon in trunks, branches, roots, leaves, and soil. Mature forests（成熟林）often contain large carbon stocks（碳储量）because carbon has accumulated over decades or centuries. When forests are cleared, burned, or degraded, stored carbon returns to the atmosphere as CO₂. This contributes to carbon emissions（碳排放）and strengthens climate pressure（气候压力）. Tropical deforestation alone accounts for approximately ten percent of global greenhouse gas emissions（温室气体排放）, making forest protection a significant component of climate mitigation（气候减缓）.

The relationship between forests and climate works in both directions. Forests influence local temperature, humidity, water movement, and carbon storage. Climate conditions influence forest growth, species distribution, fire risk, pest outbreaks, and water availability. Rising temperatures can increase evaporation（蒸发）, dry out soil, and place stress on trees. Changes in rainfall can alter seedling survival（幼苗存活）, river flow, drought frequency, and plant reproduction. Warmer conditions may allow pests（害虫）or diseases to expand into regions where they previously could not survive. Forests and climate therefore form a continuous feedback relationship（反馈关系）where each affects the other across local, regional, and global scales.

Fire is part of many forest systems. In some ecosystems, periodic fire clears dead material, releases nutrients, and helps certain seeds germinate（发芽）. Fire-adapted species（火适应物种）have evolved thick bark, serotinous cones（球果开裂机制）, or underground storage organs that allow recovery after burning. Fire becomes more destructive when climate, land use, and human activity change its frequency or intensity beyond the range that the ecosystem has adapted to. Longer dry seasons, accumulated dry vegetation, and higher temperatures can increase fire risk. Severe fires remove vegetation, expose soil, destroy habitats, and release large amounts of carbon. After intense fire, recovery depends on seed sources, soil condition, rainfall, surviving roots, and nearby species that can recolonise the burned area.

Forest degradation（森林退化）describes the gradual loss of forest quality and function. A degraded forest may still contain trees, while its ecological capacity（生态能力）has weakened. Selective logging（选择性采伐）can remove large old trees that provide nesting sites and store significant carbon. Overgrazing（过度放牧）can damage young plants and prevent regeneration（再生）. Pollution can affect soil organisms and water quality. Invasive species（入侵物种）can change competition patterns among plants and animals. Degradation often develops slowly, and tree cover alone may hide the decline of deeper ecological functions — a phenomenon sometimes called "empty forest syndrome"（空林综合征）, where the forest appears intact from above while its animal populations and ecological processes have been depleted.

Restoration（生态恢复）aims to rebuild ecological functions. Replanting trees can increase vegetation cover, and the larger task involves rebuilding soil stability, restoring native species（本地物种）, reconnecting habitats, improving water retention（水分保持）, and allowing ecological relationships to return. A successful restoration project considers species selection, local climate, soil condition, water availability, and the needs of wildlife. Planting fast-growing non-native trees may increase visible cover quickly, while restoring a diverse native forest requires more time, ecological planning, and understanding of the species interactions that make the forest function as a system.

Conservation（保护）focuses on maintaining existing ecological functions and preventing further loss. Protected areas（保护区）can preserve habitats and reduce direct human disturbance. Wildlife corridors（野生动物廊道）can connect fragmented habitats and support animal movement between patches. Monitoring（监测）allows scientists to track population changes, forest health, water quality, and recovery progress. Policy enforcement（政策执行）gives conservation rules practical force. Local cooperation（地方社区合作）helps align environmental goals with livelihoods, farming, tourism, and resource use. Conservation that excludes local communities often fails because the people who live closest to forests have the most direct influence on their condition.

Sustainable forest management（可持续森林管理）organises human use of forests within ecological limits. It recognises timber production（木材生产）, local income, biodiversity, soil protection, water regulation, and carbon storage as connected concerns. A forest can provide resources while maintaining long-term function when harvesting levels, regeneration rates, habitat protection, and community needs are balanced. This form of management treats forests as living infrastructure（生命基础设施）that supports both ecological stability and human society across generations.

Forest language grows from system function. Terms such as canopy, habitat, biodiversity, resilience, degradation, restoration, and management name the processes through which forests hold soil, regulate water, shelter species, store carbon, and maintain ecological capacity over time. Understanding these terms within their functional context allows the reader to follow how environmental texts trace the connections between forest structure, ecological function, human impact, and the strategies used to protect and restore forest systems.

## Soil, Water, and Nutrient Cycles（土壤、水分与养分循环）

Soil functions as a living system（活性系统）that supports almost all terrestrial life. It contains minerals（矿物质）, organic matter（有机质）, water, air, and billions of living organisms in a complex matrix（复杂基质）that determines how vegetation grows, how water moves, and how nutrients cycle through the ecosystem. Soil stores water, holds nutrients, provides a medium for plant roots, filters contaminants（过滤污染物）, and decomposes organic waste. Its structure and quality determine how much vegetation can grow on land and how resilient that vegetation is to drought, disease, and disturbance.

Soil forms slowly through weathering（风化作用）of rock and the accumulation of organic matter over centuries and millennia. Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller particles through temperature changes, frost action（冻融作用）, and abrasion. Chemical weathering dissolves minerals and transforms rock structure through reactions with water, oxygen, and organic acids. Biological weathering occurs when plant roots penetrate cracks in rock and when organisms produce acids that accelerate mineral breakdown. The mixture of resulting particles determines soil texture（土壤质地）. Sandy soil（沙质土壤）drains quickly but holds less water and nutrients. Clay soil（黏质土壤）holds water well but can drain too slowly and restrict root aeration（根系通气）. Loam（壤土）combines sand, silt, and clay to provide balanced drainage, water retention, and nutrient availability for plant growth.

Organic matter comes from dead plants, animals, and microorganisms. Decomposition（分解）breaks this material down into humus（腐殖质）, a stable organic substance that improves soil structure, increases water retention（水分保持）, and provides a slow-release reservoir of nutrients for plants. Earthworms（蚯蚓）, bacteria, fungi, and other soil organisms drive decomposition. They mix the soil through bioturbation（生物扰动）, break down organic material through enzymatic processes（酶促过程）, and release nutrients in forms that plants can absorb through their roots. A single teaspoon of healthy soil contains more microorganisms than there are people on Earth, and these organisms form complex food webs（食物网）that regulate nutrient availability and soil structure.

Water moves through soil in a cycle that connects precipitation（降水）, infiltration（渗透）, plant uptake（植物吸收）, and groundwater recharge（地下水补给）. Precipitation falls on land, and water either runs off the surface into rivers or infiltrates into the ground. Infiltration rate（渗透速率）depends on soil texture, structure, organic matter content, and existing moisture levels. Infiltrated water fills the pore spaces（孔隙）between soil particles. Plants absorb this water through their roots and use it for photosynthesis, nutrient transport, and temperature regulation through transpiration. Excess water moves deeper through the soil profile（土壤剖面）to recharge groundwater（地下水）or flows laterally into streams. This movement connects soil water to the wider hydrological cycle（水文循环）and determines how much water is available for plants, how much reaches rivers, and how much recharges underground aquifers（地下含水层）.

The nutrient cycle（养分循环）moves nutrients between living organisms and the physical environment. When plants and animals die, decomposers break down their bodies and release nutrients back into the soil. Plants absorb these nutrients through their roots to build new tissue. Herbivores（草食动物）get nutrients by eating plants, and carnivores（肉食动物）get nutrients by eating herbivores. When organisms die, the cycle repeats. This continuous recycling means that the same atoms of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium may pass through dozens of organisms over centuries, moving between soil, plants, animals, and microorganisms in an endless loop.

Carbon, nitrogen（氮）, phosphorus（磷）, and potassium（钾）rank among the most important nutrients for life. Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere, but most organisms cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria（固氮细菌）— including free-living soil bacteria and symbiotic bacteria（共生细菌）in the root nodules（根瘤）of leguminous plants（豆科植物）— convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium（铵）and nitrate（硝酸盐）, forms that plants can absorb. This biological nitrogen fixation（生物固氮）makes nitrogen available to the entire food chain. Phosphorus, by contrast, has no atmospheric form and cycles slowly through rock weathering, soil minerals, and biological uptake, making phosphorus availability（磷有效性）a frequent limiting factor（限制因子）for plant growth in many ecosystems.

Human activity disrupts natural nutrient cycles through multiple pathways. Agriculture removes crops from the land, taking nutrients away with each harvest. Farmers add fertilisers（化肥）to replace those nutrients, but excess fertiliser that is not absorbed by plants can run off into rivers and lakes or leach into groundwater（淋溶至地下水）. Excess nutrients in water cause eutrophication（富营养化）— a process where nutrient enrichment stimulates rapid algal growth（藻类生长）, which depletes dissolved oxygen（溶解氧）when the algae die and decompose, creating dead zones（死亡区）where aquatic life cannot survive. The global nitrogen cycle has been altered so dramatically by fertiliser production and fossil fuel combustion（化石燃料燃烧）that human activity now fixes more nitrogen than all natural terrestrial processes combined.

Soil erosion removes topsoil（表土）faster than new soil can form. Topsoil contains most of the organic matter, nutrients, and biological activity that support plant growth. When erosion removes this layer, soil fertility drops, water retention decreases, and the land can support less vegetation. Deforestation, overgrazing, and intensive farming（集约农业）without soil conservation increase erosion rates by removing the vegetation cover that protects soil from wind and water. In some agricultural regions, soil is being lost ten to forty times faster than it is being formed — a rate that threatens long-term food production capacity（粮食生产能力）.

Healthy soil supports food production, water purification（水净化）, carbon storage（碳储存）, and biodiversity. Soil conservation（土壤保护）practices — crop rotation（轮作）, contour ploughing（等高耕作）, cover cropping（覆盖种植）, reduced tillage（少耕）, and agroforestry（农林业）— help maintain soil structure and reduce erosion by keeping the soil covered, diversifying root systems, and minimising mechanical disturbance. Sustaining soil quality is essential for long-term food security（粮食安全）and environmental stability, because soil degradation is difficult to reverse on human timescales — forming just one centimetre of topsoil can take hundreds of years under natural conditions.

Soil, water, and nutrient cycles operate as interconnected systems. Soil structure determines how water moves; water movement determines which nutrients reach plant roots; nutrient availability determines how much vegetation grows; and vegetation protects soil from erosion while returning organic matter through leaf litter and root decay. Understanding these connections allows the reader to follow how environmental texts trace the pathways through which land management decisions — from farming practices to deforestation to conservation — propagate through soil, water, and nutrient systems to affect both ecological function and human wellbeing.

## Habitats and Species Survival（栖息地与物种生存）

A habitat（栖息地）provides the complete set of resources and conditions a species needs to survive and reproduce: food, water, shelter, breeding sites, suitable temperature range, and protection from predators and disease. Each species is adapted to a particular range of conditions through evolutionary processes（进化过程）that have shaped its physiology（生理特征）, behaviour（行为）, and life history（生活史）over thousands or millions of years. When the habitat changes — whether through natural disturbance or human activity — the species must adapt, move, or decline.

Different species need different kinds of habitats, and the specificity of their requirements determines their vulnerability to habitat change. A spotted owl（斑点猫头鹰）needs old-growth forests（原始林）with large trees for nesting, complex canopy structure for cover, and large foraging areas to hunt small mammals. A coral（珊瑚）needs warm, clear, shallow water with stable temperatures, adequate salinity（盐度）, and enough light for its symbiotic algae（共生藻类）to photosynthesise. A polar bear（北极熊）needs sea ice（海冰）as a platform for hunting seals（海豹）. A farmland bird（农田鸟类）needs open fields with mixed crops, hedgerows（树篱）for nesting, and abundant insects to feed its young. Each species' habitat requirements reflect its evolutionary history（进化历史）and the ecological niche（生态位）it occupies.

Habitat loss（栖息地丧失）drives species decline（物种减少）and extinction（灭绝）worldwide. When human activities clear, drain, pollute, or convert land, the habitat that supported native species disappears. Agriculture（农业）, urban development（城市发展）, logging（伐木）, mining（采矿）, and dam construction（大坝建设）are major causes. Habitat loss operates through direct destruction — clearing a forest for a plantation — and through gradual degradation — slowly changing water quality, light levels, or disturbance frequency until conditions no longer support the original species. The rate of current habitat loss is unprecedented: tropical forests are being cleared at approximately ten million hectares per year, and wetlands（湿地）have lost more than half their global area since 1900.

Habitat fragmentation（栖息地破碎化）divides large continuous habitats into smaller, isolated patches separated by human-modified landscapes. This fragmentation changes ecological processes in several ways. Small patches support fewer species and smaller populations because they contain less habitat diversity and fewer resources. Small populations are more vulnerable to extinction because they have less genetic diversity（遗传多样性）, are more sensitive to random demographic events（随机人口事件）, and are more likely to experience inbreeding depression（近交衰退）. Fragmentation also creates barriers to movement（移动障碍）. Many species need to move between habitat patches to find food, mates, or new territory. Roads, farms, and urban areas block movement and isolate populations. When populations cannot exchange genes（基因交流）, genetic diversity declines, and local extinctions are less likely to be recolonised from other areas.

Edge effects（边缘效应）emerge as a specific consequence of fragmentation. The boundary between a habitat patch and the surrounding modified landscape creates a gradient of conditions — more light, more wind, higher temperature, lower humidity, and more human disturbance near the edge. These edge conditions（边缘条件）penetrate into the habitat patch, sometimes reaching hundreds of metres into the forest interior. Species adapted to interior conditions — stable temperature, high humidity, low light, minimal disturbance — lose suitable habitat even when the patch appears to retain forest cover. The proportion of edge habitat increases as patches become smaller and more irregular in shape, meaning that small fragments may consist almost entirely of edge conditions with no true interior habitat remaining.

Habitat degradation（栖息地退化）occurs when the quality of a habitat declines even though it still physically exists. Pollution（污染）, invasive species（入侵物种）, climate change（气候变化）, noise disturbance（噪音干扰）, light pollution（光污染）, and unsustainable resource extraction can degrade habitats. A degraded habitat may still contain trees, water, and soil, but it can no longer support the native species that depend on specific conditions. A river that has been warmed by thermal pollution（热污染）from a power plant may no longer support cold-water fish species even though the river still flows. A forest where logging has removed the largest trees may still look forested but may lack the nesting cavities and canopy structure that certain bird species require.

Generalist species（广适性物种）tolerate habitat change better than specialist species（专性物种）. Generalists can use a wide range of food sources, nest in various conditions, and survive across different temperature and moisture ranges. They often thrive in human-modified landscapes. Specialists need very specific conditions — a particular food plant, a specific temperature range, a certain soil type, or a particular breeding substrate — and are more likely to decline when their habitat is altered. The global trend toward habitat loss and fragmentation therefore disproportionately affects specialist species, leading to biotic homogenisation（生物均质化）— a process where diverse local communities are replaced by the same widespread generalist species across different regions.

Conserving habitats addresses the root cause of species decline. Protected areas（保护区）can preserve large, intact habitats that maintain ecological processes and support viable populations of native species. When habitats are fragmented, wildlife corridors（野生动物廊道）can connect isolated patches and allow movement, gene flow, and recolonisation. Corridors can take many forms — forested strips along rivers, hedgerows between fields, wildlife overpasses（野生动物天桥）across highways, or underwater passages for fish. Restoring degraded habitats（恢复退化栖息地）can bring back the conditions species need by removing invasive species, replanting native vegetation, restoring natural water flows, and reducing disturbance. The survival of most species depends on maintaining the habitats they are adapted to, because species cannot evolve new habitat requirements faster than habitats are being destroyed.

Habitat ecology therefore centres on the relationship between environmental conditions and species survival. Each term — habitat, habitat loss, fragmentation, edge effect, degradation, specialist species, generalist species, protected area, wildlife corridor — names a dimension of how species depend on their environment and how human activity alters that dependence. Environmental texts build arguments through these relationships, tracing the pathways from land use change to habitat alteration to species decline and the strategies used to interrupt those pathways.

## Biodiversity and Ecosystem Resilience（生物多样性与生态系统韧性）

Biodiversity（生物多样性）captures the variety of life at all levels of biological organisation: from genetic variation（遗传变异）within populations, to species richness（物种丰富度）within ecosystems, to ecosystem diversity（生态系统多样性）across landscapes and the planet. It includes the number of species, the genetic variation within each species, the variety of ecological roles that different species perform, and the range of different ecosystem types — forests, grasslands, wetlands, coral reefs, deserts, and oceans. Biodiversity represents the accumulated product of billions of years of evolution（进化）, and it embodies the total range of solutions that life has developed to survive under different environmental conditions.

Biodiversity is distributed unevenly across the planet. Tropical regions（热带地区）contain more species than temperate or polar regions（温带或极地地区）because higher temperatures, greater solar energy, more stable climates over geological time, and more complex habitat structure support more species and more ecological niches（生态位）. Tropical rainforests（热带雨林）cover less than seven percent of the Earth's land surface but contain more than half of all known species. Coral reefs（珊瑚礁）occupy less than one percent of the ocean floor but support approximately twenty-five percent of all marine species（海洋物种）. These concentrations of biodiversity are called biodiversity hotspots（生物多样性热点）— regions that support exceptionally high numbers of species, including many endemic species（特有物种）found nowhere else, and that face significant threats from human activity.

Higher biodiversity increases ecosystem resilience（生态系统韧性）through several mechanisms. Functional diversity（功能多样性）means that more species perform different ecological roles — pollination, decomposition, nutrient fixation, predation, seed dispersal, soil aeration. When an ecosystem contains multiple species performing each function, the loss of one species can be partially compensated by others that perform a similar role. This functional redundancy（功能冗余）allows the ecosystem to continue functioning even when disturbed. In a diverse grassland（多样化草地）, drought may reduce the population of some plant species, but other species that are more drought-tolerant（耐旱的）can increase and maintain vegetation cover, forage production, and soil stability. In a less diverse grassland, there may be no drought-tolerant species to compensate, and the entire system can lose function after a severe drought.

Genetic diversity（遗传多样性）within species provides another layer of resilience. Populations with high genetic variation contain individuals with different traits — different drought tolerance, different disease resistance（抗病性）, different temperature optima（最适温度）. When environmental conditions change, some individuals are likely to possess traits that allow them to survive and reproduce under the new conditions. This genetic variation serves as the raw material（原始材料）for natural selection（自然选择）and adaptation（适应）. Populations with low genetic diversity — such as those in small, isolated habitat fragments — have less capacity to adapt to changing conditions and are more vulnerable to disease, climate change, and other pressures.

Biodiversity supports ecosystem services（生态系统服务）— the benefits that humans obtain from ecosystems. These services fall into four categories. Provisioning services（供给服务）include food, water, timber, fibre, fuel, and medicinal resources. Regulating services（调节服务）include climate regulation（气候调节）, flood control（洪水控制）, water purification, pollination（授粉）, pest control（害虫控制）, and disease regulation. Cultural services（文化服务）include recreational, aesthetic, spiritual, and educational benefits. Supporting services（支持服务）include nutrient cycling, soil formation, primary production（初级生产）, and oxygen production — the underlying processes that make all other services possible. Many of these services depend directly on biodiversity, and when biodiversity declines, the services can be reduced, degraded, or lost entirely.

Human activity is reducing biodiversity at a faster rate than at any time in human history. The current rate of species extinction（物种灭绝速率）is estimated to be hundreds to thousands of times higher than the natural background rate（自然背景速率）observed in the fossil record. The main drivers of biodiversity loss form a set of interacting pressures: habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation（过度开发）of species through hunting, fishing, and logging, introduction of invasive species（入侵物种引入）that outcompete or prey on native species, pollution of air, water, and soil, and climate change that shifts environmental conditions faster than species can adapt or migrate. These drivers often reinforce each other — habitat fragmentation makes species more vulnerable to climate change, pollution weakens populations and makes them more susceptible to disease, and overexploitation reduces population sizes and genetic diversity.

The loss of biodiversity reduces the capacity of ecosystems to respond to changes and disturbances. It also reduces the potential for future discoveries — many medicines originate from wild species（野生物种）, and the genetic resources（遗传资源）contained in biodiversity provide material for crop improvement, industrial processes, and biotechnology（生物技术）. The economic value of ecosystem services lost through biodiversity decline is estimated at trillions of dollars annually. Conserving biodiversity is therefore important for ecosystem function, human wellbeing, economic stability, and the capacity of life on Earth to adapt to future conditions.

Biodiversity therefore functions as the foundation of ecosystem resilience and the source of the services that human societies depend on. The vocabulary of biodiversity — species richness, genetic variation, functional diversity, functional redundancy, ecosystem service, biodiversity hotspot, extinction rate — names the dimensions through which life's variety supports both ecological stability and human wellbeing. Environmental texts use this vocabulary to trace the connections between human activity, biodiversity loss, and the cascading effects on ecosystem function and the services that sustain human life.

## Human Land Use and Environmental Change（人类土地使用与环境变化）

Human use of land has transformed most of the Earth's ice-free land surface. People clear forests for agriculture, build cities and roads, drain wetlands, graze livestock, mine minerals, and construct infrastructure. Approximately seventy-five percent of the Earth's ice-free land has been significantly modified by human activity. These changes alter ecological processes（生态过程）, affect biodiversity, change water and nutrient cycles, and modify the environmental services that ecosystems provide to human societies.

Agriculture（农业）represents the largest single cause of land use change. Farming converts natural ecosystems into cropland（耕地）and pasture（牧场）, simplifying the ecosystem, reducing biodiversity, and altering water and nutrient cycles. Approximately forty percent of the Earth's land surface is now used for agriculture. Intensive agriculture（集约农业）uses large amounts of fertiliser（化肥）, pesticides（杀虫剂）, irrigation water（灌溉水）, and energy to achieve high yields per unit of land. While this approach has dramatically increased food production, it has also caused soil degradation, water pollution（水污染）, aquifer depletion（含水层枯竭）, and loss of habitat for native species. The expansion of agricultural frontier（农业前沿扩张）into tropical forests — driven by global demand for soy（大豆）, palm oil（棕榈油）, beef（牛肉）, and other commodities — is a primary driver of deforestation in South America, Southeast Asia, and Central Africa.

Urbanisation（城市化）converts rural and natural land into built-up areas（建成区）with buildings, roads, and infrastructure. Urban areas increase stormwater runoff（雨水径流）because impervious surfaces（不透水表面）— concrete, asphalt, rooftops — prevent water from infiltrating into the ground. Urbanisation reduces local biodiversity by replacing native vegetation with built structures, fragments remaining habitats through road networks and development, and increases local temperatures through the urban heat island effect（城市热岛效应）— where concrete and asphalt absorb solar energy during the day and release it slowly at night, keeping urban areas several degrees warmer than surrounding rural landscapes. Cities concentrate human population and demand for resources, placing pressure on surrounding ecosystems through water extraction, waste discharge, and resource consumption.

Deforestation（森林砍伐）clears forests for other land uses — agriculture, logging, mining, or urban expansion. The process causes soil erosion（土壤侵蚀）, reduces carbon storage（碳储存）, eliminates habitats（消除栖息地）, and changes the water cycle（改变水循环）. Tropical deforestation is especially rapid today, driven by global commodity chains（全球商品链）that connect consumer demand in wealthy countries to land clearing in tropical regions. The loss of tropical forests affects global climate because these forests store enormous quantities of carbon and recycle moisture that sustains regional rainfall patterns.

Overgrazing（过度放牧）occurs when too many livestock graze an area for too long, removing vegetation faster than it can regenerate. Overgrazing removes ground cover, compacts soil through trampling（踩踏）, increases erosion, and reduces the diversity of plant species. In dry regions, overgrazing can initiate desertification（荒漠化）— a process where productive land becomes increasingly arid and unable to support vegetation or agriculture. Desertification affects approximately one-third of the Earth's land surface and threatens the livelihoods of more than one billion people who depend on dryland ecosystems（旱地生态系统）.

Land use change interacts with other environmental changes through feedback mechanisms（反馈机制）. Deforestation increases carbon emissions, which contributes to climate change. Climate change then increases the frequency of droughts and fires, which can cause further forest loss. Nutrient runoff from agriculture creates dead zones in coastal waters, which reduces fish populations and affects the livelihoods of fishing communities. These interactions can create positive feedbacks（正反馈）— self-reinforcing cycles where one change amplifies another — that accelerate environmental degradation beyond what any single driver would produce alone.

Sustainable land use（可持续土地使用）aims to meet human needs while maintaining ecological functions. Agroforestry（农林业）combines trees with crops or livestock, maintaining many ecological benefits — soil protection, carbon storage, habitat provision — while producing food and income. Organic farming（有机农业）reduces synthetic chemical inputs and often supports higher on-farm biodiversity. Conservation agriculture（保护性农业）minimises soil disturbance, maintains permanent soil cover, and diversifies crop rotations to protect soil health. Protected areas（保护区）preserve natural ecosystems while providing recreational, cultural, and ecological benefits. The challenge of sustainable land use is to manage the competing demands for food production, housing, infrastructure, resource extraction, and ecological conservation within the finite area of the Earth's land surface.

Human land use therefore represents the primary force reshaping the Earth's surface and the ecological processes that sustain life. The vocabulary of land use — agriculture, urbanisation, deforestation, overgrazing, desertification, feedback mechanism, sustainable land use — names the pathways through which human activity transforms natural systems and the strategies used to manage that transformation. Environmental texts trace these pathways from land use decisions through ecological consequences to policy responses, allowing the reader to follow how human societies interact with the natural systems on which they depend.

## Conservation and Ecological Restoration（保护与生态恢复）

Conservation（保护）functions as the practice of protecting and managing nature to maintain biodiversity, ecosystem functions, and the services that ecosystems provide. Conservation operates at multiple scales — from protecting individual species（物种保护）to preserving entire ecosystems（生态系统保护）— and uses a range of strategies depending on the threats, the species involved, and the social and economic context.

Species-focused conservation（物种层面保护）targets endangered species（濒危物种）that face high risk of extinction. It includes measures like protecting remaining habitats（保护剩余栖息地）, preventing poaching（防止偷猎）and illegal trade, managing populations through monitoring and intervention, and in some cases captive breeding（人工繁殖）programmes to increase population numbers before releasing individuals back into the wild. The recovery of the giant panda（大熊猫）, the bald eagle（白头鹰）, and the Arabian oryx（阿拉伯羚羊）demonstrates that targeted conservation can bring species back from the brink of extinction when sufficient resources, political will, and scientific knowledge are applied.

Ecosystem-focused conservation（生态系统层面保护）protects entire habitats and the ecological processes they support. Protected areas（保护区）— national parks（国家公园）, nature reserves（自然保护区）, wilderness areas（荒野区）, marine protected areas（海洋保护区）— are the primary tool. These areas limit or prohibit human activities that damage ecosystems — logging, mining, hunting, industrial development — allowing native species and ecological processes to persist. Well-managed protected areas can maintain biodiversity, store carbon, regulate water, and provide habitat for species that cannot survive in human-modified landscapes. The global network of protected areas now covers approximately fifteen percent of the Earth's land surface and eight percent of the ocean, though many protected areas lack adequate management, enforcement, or connectivity to fully achieve their conservation goals.

Protected areas alone are insufficient because many ecosystems are already degraded or fragmented outside their boundaries, and species need to move across landscapes to maintain genetic diversity and respond to climate change. Conservation must therefore work across the entire landscape（全景观保护）, integrating protected areas with sustainable land use in surrounding areas. Wildlife corridors（野生动物廊道）connect isolated protected areas and allow animal movement, gene flow, and ecological processes to operate at landscape scales. Buffer zones（缓冲区）around protected areas reduce edge effects and provide transitional areas where human activity is managed to be compatible with conservation goals. Community-based conservation（社区保护）involves local people in conservation planning and ensures that conservation provides tangible benefits to the communities that live closest to protected ecosystems.

Ecological restoration（生态恢复）repairs degraded, damaged, or destroyed ecosystems by rebuilding the ecological processes, native species communities, and physical conditions that existed before degradation. Restoration can take many forms depending on the type and severity of degradation. Reforestation（重新造林）plants trees to restore forest cover and rebuild habitat structure. Wetland restoration（湿地恢复）involves rewetting drained wetlands, restoring natural hydrology（自然水文）, and reintroducing native plant species. River restoration（河流恢复）removes dams, reconnects floodplains（重新连接洪泛区）, and restores natural flow regimes. Soil restoration（土壤恢复）improves soil structure and fertility through organic matter addition, reduced tillage, and cover cropping after periods of erosion or contamination.

Successful restoration follows ecological principles（生态学原则）. It considers the local climate, soil conditions, hydrology, native species composition（物种组成）, and the natural disturbance regime that shaped the ecosystem. Restoration typically requires addressing the underlying cause of degradation before species can recover — restoring natural water flow before replanting wetland species, removing invasive species（清除入侵物种）before reintroducing native ones, or stabilising soil before planting trees. Active restoration（主动恢复）involves direct human intervention — planting, seeding, removing barriers, reintroducing species. Passive restoration（被动恢复）, also called natural regeneration（自然再生）, involves removing the cause of degradation and allowing the ecosystem to recover through natural processes, which can be slower but often produces more ecologically authentic results.

The global commitment to restoration has grown significantly. The United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration（联合国生态系统恢复十年）and national commitments from many countries have set targets to restore hundreds of millions of hectares of degraded land. Achieving these targets requires sustained investment, scientific guidance, community engagement, and long-term monitoring to ensure that restored ecosystems develop the resilience and biodiversity needed to persist under future conditions. Conserving what remains and restoring what has been lost together form the two pillars of maintaining biodiversity, ecosystem services, and the ecological foundation that supports both human society and the natural world.

Conservation and restoration therefore represent complementary approaches to maintaining ecological function in a world shaped by human activity. Conservation preserves what still functions; restoration rebuilds what has been damaged. The vocabulary of conservation — protected area, wildlife corridor, buffer zone, community-based conservation, ecological restoration, active restoration, natural regeneration — names the strategies through which societies attempt to maintain and repair the ecological systems on which all life depends. Environmental texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from ecological degradation through conservation and restoration strategies to the outcomes that determine whether ecosystems can persist under future conditions.

## Sustainable Development and Ecological Limits（可持续发展与生态边界）

Sustainable development（可持续发展）meets the needs of the present while preserving the ability of future generations（后代）to meet their own needs. This concept, established by the Brundtland Commission（布伦特兰委员会）in 1987, recognises that economic development（经济发展）and human wellbeing depend on a healthy environment（健康环境）and functioning ecosystems（运行中的生态系统）. Degrading the planet's life-support systems — its atmosphere, oceans, forests, soils, and freshwater — undermines the conditions for long-term prosperity and increases the vulnerability of the poorest populations, who depend most directly on natural resources.

Ecological limits（生态边界）define how much humans can extract from the environment, how much waste the environment can absorb, and how much disturbance ecosystems can withstand before they shift into fundamentally different states. Scientists have identified several critical planetary boundaries（行星边界）that define a safe operating space for humanity: climate change（气候变化）, biodiversity loss（生物多样性丧失）, nitrogen and phosphorus pollution（氮磷污染）, land system change（土地系统变化）, freshwater use（淡水使用）, ocean acidification（海洋酸化）, ozone depletion（臭氧消耗）, atmospheric aerosol loading（大气气溶胶负荷）, and chemical pollution（化学污染）. Crossing these boundaries risks irreversible change（不可逆变化）that undermines the stability of the Earth system（地球系统）that has supported human civilisation for the past ten thousand years. Current evidence suggests that several of these boundaries — climate change, biodiversity loss, nitrogen cycling, and land system change — have already been exceeded.

Sustainable development requires balancing three interconnected goals: economic development（经济发展）— improving human living standards and reducing poverty; social development（社会发展）— ensuring equity, access to resources, education, healthcare, and social wellbeing; and environmental protection（环境保护）— conserving the natural resources and ecosystems that support life. These goals can conflict in the short term — protecting a forest may limit logging jobs, and regulating emissions may increase production costs — but they are mutually dependent（相互依赖）in the long term. Economies depend on natural resources and ecosystem services. Social stability depends on both economic opportunity and environmental quality. Environmental protection depends on economic resources and social support for conservation policies.

The concept of the circular economy（循环经济）illustrates how sustainable development can align economic and environmental goals. In a linear economy（线性经济）, resources are extracted, transformed into products, used, and discarded as waste. In a circular economy, materials are kept in use through recycling（回收）, reuse（再利用）, repair（修复）, and remanufacturing（再制造）. Waste from one process becomes input for another. This approach reduces resource extraction, decreases pollution, creates economic value from materials that would otherwise be discarded, and reduces the pressure on natural ecosystems that supply raw materials and absorb waste.

The energy transition（能源转型）from fossil fuels（化石燃料）to renewable energy（可再生能源）illustrates how sustainable development requires systemic change（系统性变革）. Replacing coal, oil, and natural gas with solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal energy reduces greenhouse gas emissions（温室气体排放）, improves air quality（空气质量）, creates new industries and employment, and reduces dependence on finite resources. The transition requires enormous investment in new infrastructure, retraining of workers in fossil fuel industries, and policy frameworks that support clean energy deployment — illustrating how environmental, economic, and social dimensions of sustainability are interconnected.

Inequity（不平等）represents a persistent challenge for sustainable development. Wealthy countries and wealthy individuals consume disproportionate shares of natural resources and produce disproportionate shares of pollution and emissions. Poor countries and poor individuals, who have contributed least to environmental degradation, often suffer the most severe consequences — exposure to pollution, vulnerability to climate change, loss of livelihood resources, and displacement by environmental disasters（环境灾难）. Addressing this inequity requires that sustainable development policies consider distribution（分配）— who benefits, who bears the costs, and how the transition to sustainability can be made fair across populations and generations.

Sustainable development therefore centres on the relationship between human needs and ecological limits. The vocabulary of sustainability — ecological limits, planetary boundaries, circular economy, energy transition, inequity, distribution — names the concepts through which societies attempt to balance economic development, social equity, and environmental protection. Environmental texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from human activity through ecological consequences to the policy choices that determine whether development can continue within the boundaries that the Earth's systems can sustain.
